23.0.0.en: 1 Then Job answered and said, 2 "Even to day is my complaint rebellion: my stroke is heavier than my groaning. 3 Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat! 4 I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments. 5 I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me."

23.1.0.en: "Even to day is my complaint rebellion: my stroke is heavier than my groaning" [2].

23.1.1.en: Job says that his complaint is bitter. His friends reckoned it rebellion against God, but Job gives a justification for his complaint, which is that however much he groans, the groanings of his heart cannot express how heavy his calamities are. The wounds of his body and soul are exceedingly severe, and they justify his complaint.

23.1.2.en: * The pains of the afflicted man ought to be healed by the comfort of his friends, but because their comfort carried deceit, the pains of the stricken man became harsher than they were. Eliphaz did not hide his intention, as he promises better things if he repents; this was like a poisoned remedy, and the wound grew worse.

23.1.4.en: * "A faithful friend is the medicine of life" (Sir 6:16).

23.1.5.en: There is no remedy so effective in healing pains as the sincere friend who comforts you in your afflictions, manages your problems, rejoices in your success and grieves in your calamities. Whoever has found such a friend has found a treasure. For a faithful friend has no equal, and no weight of gold and silver can balance the goodness of his faithfulness (see Sir 6:14-15).

23.1.6.en: * Nothing establishes love so strongly as sharing in joy and pain. Do not, because you are far from troubles, isolate yourself also from sharing with others. When your neighbor is in distress, reckon the distress as your own. Share his tears to support his crushed spirit, and share his joy so that the joy in him becomes deep and rooted.

23.1.7.en: Establish love, for by this you serve yourself more than you serve him. By your tears you become merciful, and by feelings of gladness you purify your soul from envy and gloom... If you cannot remove evils from him, share them with him by your tears, and you will remove half the evil from him; and if you cannot increase his goods, share his joy and you will add something great to him.

23.1.8.en: St. John Chrysostom "My stroke is heavier than my groaning"; and in Pope Gregory (the Great) it came: "The hand of my stroke is heavier than my groaning." Here he means the blow that struck him at the hands of his friends who opposed him, for it is more violent than the trials that came upon him and drove him to groan. It is as though his friends, instead of comforting him to calm his groanings, inflamed the wounds, for their hands came more violently than what had befallen him. The son of Sirach says: "There is a companion who rejoices with his friend in prosperity, and in adversity becomes his enemy" (Sir 37:4).

23.2.0.en: "Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat!" [3]

23.2.1.en: Job was confident of God's justice and longed to stand before His throne to complain to Him, for He would surely do him justice and would not crush him as his friends had done. As David the prophet says: "I am in a great strait: let us fall now into the hand of the LORD; for his mercies are great: and let me not fall into the hand of man" (2 Sam 24:14).

23.2.2.en: Perhaps Job felt that sin had separated him from God and that his weaknesses had spoiled his relationship with God, so he wanted to restore this relationship and enjoy his love for God. Therefore he cries out: "Oh that I knew where I might find him!" As the human soul says: "Saw ye him whom my soul loveth?" (Song 3:3) Who will grant me to find Him? Who will open for me the way to Him?

23.2.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that Job longed to stand before God and His servants of the heavenly orders, where he would taste love and mercy, instead of what he suffered from men of his own kind. Therefore he says: "that I might come even to his seat!"

23.2.4.en: * What is the "seat" of God but the angelic spirits, whom the Holy Bible testifies are called "thrones"? Who desires to come to the seat of God but he who longs to be among the angelic spirits... so that he is lifted up to dwell in glory by contemplating eternity... For when he sees with the eyes of faith the Creator of all things ruling the angelic spirits, then he comes to His seat.

23.2.6.en: When the believer enjoys fellowship with the heavenly beings, he feels that his relationship with them is no less than his relationship with his brethren in humanity, if it does not exceed it in tenderness, mercy and love. They rejoice at his salvation, and in the name of humanity they sing the hymns of salvation, as though the salvation were their own.

23.2.7.en: * Today the King of glory is glorified on earth, as the prophet says, and makes us who dwell on earth partakers in the heavenly feast, to show that He is Lord of both (of the heavenly and the earthly). So He is praised with common hymns from both.

23.2.8.en: Therefore the heavenly orders sang, proclaiming salvation on earth: [Holy, holy, holy, Lord of Sabaoth, His glory fills all the earth](a).

23.2.9.en: And those below, as they share in the joyful hymns of heaven in harmony with them, cry out: "Hosanna in the highest, Hosanna to the Son of David."

23.3.0.en: Fr. Methodius "I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments" [4].

23.3.1.en: Job longs to present his case to God, for He will surely give him the opportunity to defend himself. Since Job represents the persecuted Church, though the world troubles her, she can in Christ Jesus stand before the throne with boldness and confidence, since she bears His divine righteousness, as the Apostle says.

23.3.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) translates this verse: "I would order my cause before God, and fill my mouth with reproofs." For the believer finds it good to stand before God and bring his case, where the soul discovers itself and comes to know itself more precisely, and trembles.

23.3.3.en: How different is man's attack upon the believer to crush him from the Spirit of God's disclosing to man to expose him before himself, to reprove him and to give him true repentance as a way to enjoy the Kingdom of God. We have "boldness to enter into the holiest" (Heb 10:19), and we stand before the throne of divine grace.

23.3.4.en: In open conversation with God, man accuses himself, and so is justified in God's eyes. The Lord Himself says: "Put me in remembrance: let us plead together: declare thou, that thou mayest be justified" (Isa 43:26). And the text came in the Septuagint: "Declare first your transgressions, that you may be justified" (Isa 43:26) LXX.

23.3.5.en: * God opens to us many ways to accomplish this. For He says: "Declare first your transgressions, that you may be justified" (Isa 43:26) LXX. He also says: [I said, I will tell my iniquity to You, and You take away the iniquity of my heart] (see Ps 32:5). For the constant accusation of ourselves, or the remembering of sins, contributes not a little to lessening their guilt.

23.3.6.en: * There is another way that gives us this remedy, which is to judge ourselves for our faults, because: "Declare first your transgressions, that you may be justified" (Isa 43:26) LXX. Whoever is in afflictions and gives thanks has his sins loosed, and also by almsgiving, which is greater than everything.

23.4.0.en: St. John Chrysostom "I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me" [5].

23.4.1.en: Job's friends misunderstood his questions about the reason for his falling under successive bitter trials. They counted them as a complaint against God, even as practical atheism. And they counted his questions about the success of the wicked as an attack on divine justice. But Job was confident that if he entered into judgment with God, God's answers to his questions would surely be entirely comforting and not provoking. Therefore he longed for dialogue with Him, and to submit to His judgments with complete submission. Dialogue with God is easier and sweeter than with men.

23.4.2.en: Perhaps Job is saying to his friends: I do not care much about your opinion of me, I only want to talk with God, for what concerns me is what God says about me and how He answers my questions. As the Apostle Paul says: "But with me it is a very small thing that I should be judged of you, or of man's judgment: yea, I judge not mine own self... but he that judgeth me is the Lord" (1 Cor 4:3-4).

23.4.3.en: * Paul does not mean here (1 Cor 4:4) that he is without blame, but wants to stop the mouths of those who blame him without discernment. God is our Judge, and He alone knows for certain what goes on in our hearts.

23.5.0.en: "Will he plead against me with his great power? No;

23.5.1.en: but he would give heed to me" [6].

23.5.2.en: Truly, who can enter into a dispute with God, when it is written: "the weakness of God is stronger than men" (1 Cor 1:25)? And yet dialogue with Him is better than dialogue with the sons of men, because He cares for the one who complains and listens to him as a tender father to his son. Though He is firm, with firmness He declares His tender fatherhood to the son wounded by trials and afflictions.

23.5.3.en: Job believed that Almighty God would not terrify him, and that even in his judgment and conversation with him He would not display the perfection of His majesty and greatness, but would condescend and show him as much as he could bear, so that he could converse with Him. He would not be violent with him, for He is not like the sons of men. He is longsuffering, and listens to the one who cries to Him, and strengthens and encourages him. He gives him strength, and enters with him into a struggle not to defeat him but to give him victory, as was said of our father Jacob: "by his strength he had power with God: yea, he had power over the angel, and prevailed: he wept, and made supplication unto him: he found him in Bethel, and there he spake with us" (Hos 12:3-4).

23.5.4.en: Truly, whoever has tasted true companionship with God does not cease to meet with Him, for he perceives His tenderness, His longsuffering and His condescension for the sake of His beloved man, saying with righteous Job: "Will he plead against me with his great power? No; but he would give heed to me" (Job 23:6).

23.5.5.en: * They thought that my light burden was very heavy, but I bowed down to them, leaving the Kingdom of Heaven, to eat with them, taking the human form. Rather, I gave them my body as food: I was food for them and a partner with them at the table.

23.6.s.en: 3. His assurance of victory by the Cross

23.6.0.en: "There the righteous might dispute with him; so should I be delivered for ever from my judge" [7].

23.6.1.en: Job believed that the divine judgment is issued with uprightness, and that He would deliver him on an eternal level. By taking refuge in Him we escape eternal judgment. As St. Augustine says, we flee from divine justice by taking refuge in God Himself.

23.6.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) translates this verse thus: "Let Him do justice against me, and my judgment will come to victory." And he sees in this cry the Church asking God the Word to accomplish justice by the Cross, to come down to her and redeem her; then, as she enters into the judgment, she enjoys victory on an eternal level. She asks for the Word to come to reprove her, for by His Incarnation and His reproof of her the gates of divine grace open before her, and she is justified before the divine throne.

23.6.3.en: * "Let Him do justice against me, and my judgment will come to victory"... To reprove my ways let the incarnate Son be sent... For if the only-begotten Son of God had remained unseen in the power of His divinity (that is, had not become incarnate) and had not taken anything of our weakness (our humanity), how could weak men have found the means to obtain divine grace? For the weight of His majesty, if it be considered, would in fact be against us and not for our help. But the Mighty One, who is above all, came as one weak among us, and by equaling Himself to us, taking our weakness, He raises us to His power. For it was not possible for us to perceive the loftiness of His divine nature, we ourselves being unfit for it, but He bowed down to man through His humanity, and it became possible for us to ascend, as it were, to Him who came down. He rose, and we were raised.

23.6.5.en: * Flee to God Himself, if you want to flee from Him.

23.6.6.en: Flee by confession, not by hiding.

23.6.7.en: Say to Him: [You are a refuge to me](b).

23.6.8.en: So let the love that alone gives life grow within you.

23.6.9.en: * Joyful is the face of the Lord; once it is seen, man finds his delight in nothing else.

23.7.s.en: 4. His failure to comprehend the mystery of God

23.7.0.en: "Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him [8]. On the left hand, where he doth work, but I cannot behold him:

23.8.0.en: he turneth himself to the right hand, that I cannot see him" [9].

23.8.1.en: Job expressed the bewilderment in which he was, as one who searches for God and does not find Him in the east, nor perceive Him in the west. Eliphaz had earlier commanded him to get acquainted with God (Job 22:12), and Job answers him that this is the desire of his heart, for he longs to appear before Him.

23.8.2.en: Job undoubtedly believed that God is present in every place, but here he complains of his inability to fix his thoughts on God and on His wisdom amid their pursuit of him with useless and provoking arguments. Though he believed in God's existence, it was as though something like a veil covered his inner sight, so that he was unable to recognize the reasons for his troubles that God permitted. He knew of no particular sin he had committed that he should repent of. He did not realize what God's purpose was in allowing him these calamities. And finally he did not know what the end of these calamities would be, whether God would deliver him from them. When? And how would this be accomplished?

23.8.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us more than one interpretation of the east, west, north (or left) and south (or right) in this passage.

23.8.4.en: The first interpretation: God is everywhere, and He is indivisible, filling all, seeing man and knowing all that is in his depths, but man does not see Him and cannot distinguish Him by the senses. He is awesome though unseen.

23.8.5.en: The second interpretation: if we look to the east, that is, if we think of His majesty, since He rises from the east, we cannot comprehend His nature with our mortal mind. And if we look to the west, that is, if the sight of the heart fails because of the abundance of His splendor, He cannot be understood. And if we walk toward the left, where there is falling into sins, we do not perceive Him. And if we walk toward the right, where there are the right-hand blows of pride, hypocrisy and self-righteousness, we do not see Him.

23.8.6.en: * "Behold, if I go to the east, He does not appear; and if I go to the west, I do not understand Him. If I go to the north, what shall I do? I do not perceive Him; and if I turn to the right (south), I do not see Him" [8-9]. The Creator of all things is indivisible, and He is in every place... For the incomprehensible Spirit contains everything in Himself, He who at the same time fills and contains...

23.8.7.en: It is as though he were saying plainly: I cannot look upon the One who sees me, the One who looks upon me with all exactness; I have no power to look at Him... Our Creator, who is wholly perfect in every place and distinguishes everything, cannot be distinguished (by the senses), and He is the more awesome in that He remains unseen, and the outcome of our actions hangs in the balance, and their time is unknown.

23.8.8.en: These words can also be understood in another sense: we go east when we lift up our minds by thinking of His majesty, but He "does not appear," since He cannot be seen in His nature by a mortal mind. [If I go to the west, I do not understand Him](c); we go west when the eye of the heart that was lifted up in God draws back because of the abundance of light...

23.8.9.en: To go to the left (north) is man's submission to the pleasures of his sins. It is certainly clear that the person who still pleases his sins and throws himself toward the left cannot comprehend God...

23.8.10.en: A person goes toward the right (south) who is exalted over virtuous achievements.

23.8.11.en: But God cannot be seen by the one who is pleased to enjoy his good works selfishly, for he lowers the eye of the heart by the vanity of pride. Therefore it is well said everywhere: [Thou shalt not decline... to the right hand, nor to the left] (see Deut 17:11)...

23.8.13.en: * You cannot see God, but you have the right to see Him by your love for your neighbor. And by looking to the source of that love you see God as far as you are able.

23.9.s.en: 5. His assurance that God purifies him by fire

23.9.0.en: 10 "But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold. 11 My foot hath held his steps, his way have I kept, and not declined. 12 Neither have I gone back from the commandment of his lips; I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food. 13 But he is alone, and who can turn him? and what his soul desireth, even that he doeth."

23.9.1.en: "But he knoweth the way that I take:

23.9.2.en: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold" [10].

23.9.3.en: Job acknowledged the surpassing perfection of God, who fills all and knows all. He sees even the depths, and man does not see Him. Wherever man goes, whether east or west, north or south, he cannot see God, nor comprehend His divine mysteries and His plan for every man, but he knows one thing: that in God's eyes he is reckoned precious gold that needs purifying by the fire of trials to grow in purity and splendor. For despite the extreme bewilderment that came upon Job and his not perceiving what lay behind the events in the mind of God, he knows that God knows his way, and that He will bring him out of the trial pure like gold refined by fire; and that his trial is to test or prove his faith (1 Pet 1:7).

23.9.4.en: * "And He will test me like gold that passes through the fire." Gold in the furnace advances in the splendor of its nature, while it loses the dross. So as gold passes through the fire, the souls of the righteous are tried... By the fire of trial, again and again, their faults are removed, and their virtues increase.

23.9.5.en: It is not in pride that the saint compares himself to gold tested by trials... when he thinks of himself that he has been purified by the pain of trial, even if there was nothing found in him to be purified from.

23.9.7.en: * When God wants to give victory to a man and magnify him, He first delivers him to evil (trials) to be tested and examined, and then his beauty appears to the world by the good things that God does with him.

23.9.8.en: When God wanted to give Joseph victory and make him lord over Egypt..., what was the beginning of His work to lead to a good end? First his brothers seized him, insulted him, mocked him, stripped his garments, left him in the pit, cut off his hope, and sold him to merchants, and he became a slave serving masters, and the handsome son of free men who had committed no wrong was enslaved.

23.9.9.en: Whoever saw this evil work could not have thought that all these evils were being committed for Joseph's good. But God, who knew what He wanted to do for him, did not spare him when he was being crushed under all these evils, but let him fall into the pit, be sold to the merchants, and be thrown into prison unjustly. After all these things his beauty shone like the sun, his right appeared like gold, his evils vanished like smoke, and he mounted to the top of the chariot like a king, and rose up in the greatness for which God had set him, so that by humbling himself he might be exalted.

23.9.10.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh * As the refiner of gold throws the piece of gold into the furnace to endure the fire for a time, until he sees that it has been purified, so God permits the testing of human souls with afflictions until they are purified and gain great benefit...

23.9.11.en: May we not be disturbed or despair when trials come upon us. For just as the refiner of gold knows the time for which the gold must be left in the furnace, and brings it out at the appointed time and does not leave it any longer in the fire lest it be spoiled and burned, how much more does God know this. So when He sees that we have been purified the more, He frees us from our trials so that we are not cast down and driven out because of the increase of our evils.

23.9.12.en: When something happens to us that we did not expect, let us not murmur nor let our hearts faint, but receive it from God, who knows these things exactly, so that He may test our hearts by fire as it pleases Him, since this is done for the benefit of those who are tried. Therefore the wise man commands us to submit to God in all things, because He knows perfectly when to bring us out of the furnace of evil (Sir 1:1-2).

23.9.13.en: It is fitting for us to submit to Him always, and to thank Him continually, bearing everything willingly, whether He grants us blessings or offers us chastenings. For the latter are a kind of blessing.

23.9.14.en: The physician is not only one who lets us bathe (in the baths)... or go to pleasant gardens, but also when he uses the scalpel and the knife he is a physician!

23.9.15.en: And the father is not only when he caresses his son, but also when he disciplines and punishes him... he is a father!

23.9.16.en: And since we know that God is more tender than all physicians, it is not for us to investigate His dealings, nor to demand an account from Him of them, but what is good in His eyes He does. So we do not distinguish whether He frees us from trial or disciplines us, because by both ways He wants to restore us to health and make us partners with Him, and He knows our different needs, and what suits each one of us, and how, and in what way we must be saved...

23.9.17.en: Let us follow Him wherever He commands us, and not think much whether He commands us to walk an easy, smooth road or a hard, rough one.

23.9.18.en: St. John Chrysostom * As gold is tried by fire and becomes useful, so you who live in the world are tried by it. So you who are in the fire pass through the flame and are purified. And as the dross is cast off from the gold, so you will cast off every sorrow and trial, and become pure and useful for the building of the tower.

23.9.19.en: Hermas "My foot hath held his steps,

23.10.0.en: his way have I kept, and not declined" [11].

23.10.1.en: While Job acknowledges that he needs the dross to be removed from him, he returns and declares that he has set it in his heart to walk according to God's purposes and plans, committing himself to walk in the divine way step by step. He does not want to turn aside from the way to the right or to the left.

23.10.2.en: On one hand Job rejects what his friends claim, that these trials are the fruit of his evils, his hypocrisy and his secret opposition to God, but are a crucible to purify his depths so that he comes forth as gold refined by fire; and on the other hand he declares that he walks in the way of the Lord, keeps the Lord's commandments and does not turn aside from them.

23.10.3.en: * "My foot holds fast to His steps," for the works of God that we see are a kind of traces of His steps. By these works the good and the bad are judged, the righteous and the wicked are placed in their ranks... The Truth commands us to imitate the traces of the steps of His Father, saying: pray for them which persecute you and falsely accuse you, that ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven (Mt 5:44-45)... Peter says of these His steps: [because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps] (1 Pet 2:21)...

23.10.4.en: "His way have I kept, and not declined": whoever practices what his mind has resolved keeps the way and does not turn aside from it. For he who "keeps" what he has resolved does not turn aside from it in his practical conduct. This is what occupies the righteous: that they are committed to test their conduct by the ways of truth day by day, and reckon them a rule for themselves, binding them not to turn aside from their straight path.

23.10.6.en: * Christ taught you to suffer, and He did this by suffering Himself. Words are not enough unless a practical example is added to them. What precious teaching He gave us, brothers and sisters! He was hung on the Cross, and the Jews were raging... He was hanging there, and at the same time He was healing them.

23.10.7.en: St. Augustine "Neither have I gone back from the commandment of his lips;

23.11.0.en: I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my appointed portion" [12].

23.11.1.en: Job declares that he did not turn back from the divine commandment issued from the divine mouth, but advances according to it and always strives toward the goal.

23.11.2.en: He held fast to the commandment, counting it better than his necessary food, for he cannot live without it; it is the food and drink of his soul.

23.11.3.en: Job looks upon the divine commandment as issuing from the lips of God and as the word of His mouth, so it is not mere orders by which he is bound to direct his conduct, but a sweet and precious gift issuing from the mouth of that Lover! Therefore it is not a burden that he wants to flee from, but in sweetness he does not depart from it, and in longing he lays it up in his depths. As the Psalmist says: "I have rejoiced in the way of thy testimonies, as much as in all riches. I will meditate in thy precepts, and have respect unto thy ways. I will delight myself in thy statutes: I will not forget thy word... The law of thy mouth is better unto me than thousands of gold and silver... O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day. Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. Thy testimonies have I taken as an heritage for ever: for they are the rejoicing of my heart. My tongue shall speak of thy word: for all thy commandments are righteousness" (Ps 119:14-16, 72, 97, 105, 111, 172)

23.11.4.en: * If Job had set for himself a rule, which was to walk as is fitting for him as a man, yet more precious than this rule is the divine commandment, as his treasure which he possesses and guards and keeps in his heart. [I hid the words of His mouth in the bosom of my heart]. For we hide the words in the bosom of our hearts when we hear His commandments, not in a passing way, but fulfill them in practice. It is written of the Virgin Mother herself: [But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart] (Lk 2:19).

23.11.6.en: * Truly, whoever obtains material wealth rejoices because of this wealth, not when he has a part of the wealth, but when he obtains "all riches," all the fixed and circulating assets, that is, real estate and money. So also whoever desires spiritual wealth rejoices and is glad when he obtains complete wealth, by virtue of his progress in the testimonies of the Lord and his practice of the virtues. It is as though he were saying: Let Your testimonies be what makes me need nothing else, let them be my joy and my wealth.

23.11.7.en: Origen * Those whose citizenship is in heaven (Phil 3:19-20), as long as they dwell here occupied (with the heavenly things), are truly strangers. Let them pray that God's commandments may not be hidden from them, by which they are set free during their temporary journey, by their love for God with whom they will dwell eternally; and by their love for their neighbor so that he too may go to where they will be (that is, in heaven).

23.11.8.en: St. Augustine "But he is alone, and who can turn him?

23.12.0.en: and what his soul desireth, even that he doeth" [13].

23.12.1.en: With Job's sense of his human weakness, and at the same time being unable to ignore his faithfulness and earnestness in keeping the Lord's commandments and his surpassing esteem for them, he wanted to enter into dialogue with God to learn His divine purposes behind what had befallen him.

23.12.2.en: But Job realizes his limits, that he is a weak creature who does not reproach in order to change God's plan, and does not expect to oppose God. He knows that God is the Almighty, the Wise, the Father; what He wants is for good, and He is able to do it. It is as though Job wanted, in his dialogue, God to open his insight further so that he might swim in God's surpassing love even if afflictions pursued him from every side. By this dialogue Job benefits, so that his faith and love increase and he rises above words.

23.12.3.en: God is the absolute Truth; His counsel does not change, no one shares counsel with Him, there is none to change His will and purposes. Truly He pardons upon repentance, but His purposes do not change: "all his works are known unto the Lord from the beginning of the world."

23.12.4.en: He is almighty; what He desires He accomplishes. He is not like men who desire many things which they do not do, or cannot do, or do not dare to do, for He is all-powerful. "Whatsoever the LORD pleased, that did he" (Ps 135:6).

23.12.5.en: * "If He is judged, who is this that opposes Him? For He wills a thing and accomplishes it." Knowledge is kept within the limits of nature by all its ways, but faith makes its journey above nature... The man who follows faith becomes at once free and ruler of himself, and as a son subjects all the natures of creation as though he were a god, for by faith authority in the likeness of God is realized, to establish a new creation. He says: "You do what You will, and all things are present before You." And many times faith can bring everything out of nothing.

23.12.6.en: St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian Pope Gregory (the Great) comments on the expression [He alone], as though there were no being other than He, saying that it is fitting to distinguish between the self-existent, unchangeable Creator and the creatures that came into being from nothing and cannot subsist by themselves.

23.12.7.en: * "But He is Himself alone, and no man can change His mind"... Since there is a multitude of things in the circle of nature, why is it said by the voice of the blessed man: [He alone]? There is a difference between what exists and what exists originally, between what is subject to change and existence and what is independent of change. For all these things exist, but they do not subsist by themselves; if they were not upheld by the hand of Him who governs them they could never exist at all. For all things subsist in Him who made them, and they do not owe their life to themselves, nor have those who move and do not live come to have motion according to their whims. Rather it is (God) who moves all things, He who gives life to some, granting them life, while the other beings that are without life He preserves, lodging them in a wonderful way as lesser and lower beings.

23.12.8.en: All things were created out of nothing, and their existence ends in nothing, unless the Creator of things holds them with the hand of His providence. So all created things cannot by themselves subsist, nor move, but must submit to their Former, and only in this way do they move...

23.12.9.en: In any case, even if there is opposition against us from outside (that is, afflictions), it is fitting for us to realize that God works in us from within...

23.12.10.en: So in all cases God is regarded as the One who alone is, He who exists from the beginning and who said to Moses: [I AM THAT I AM: thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you] (Ex 3:14). So when we are chastened by the things that we see, we must fear Him whom we do not see...

23.12.11.en: Concerning His immutability, he added in a direct and fitting way: "no man can change His mind," for since He is by nature unchangeable, He is unchangeable in will. "No one can change His mind," for no man has authority to resist His hidden judgments... So it is written: "He issues a decree that does not change." And also: "Heaven and earth shall pass away: but my words shall not pass away" (Mk 13:31). Also: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isa 55:8)...

23.12.12.en: For even those things that seem to be done against His will and contrary to it, let us look to this: that what He has not commanded is sometimes permitted to be done so that it may serve what He has commanded and accomplish it with greater certainty. For the will of the opposing angel is evil, but God commands in a wonderful way so that God uses his very deceitful devices for the good of the righteous who are purified through their struggle. Therefore [whatever His soul desires, He does], using the very source that may seem to oppose His will to accomplish His will by it...

23.13.0.en: 14 "For he performeth the thing that is appointed for me: and many such things are with him. 15 Therefore am I troubled at his presence: when I consider, I am afraid of him. 16 For God maketh my heart soft, and the Almighty troubleth me: 17 Because I was not cut off before the darkness, neither hath he covered the darkness from my face."

23.13.1.en: "For he performeth the thing that is appointed for me: and many such things are with him" [14].

23.13.2.en: Job looks to God, the One, the only Almighty, existing by Himself, as the source of his life and the mover of all things by His surpassing providence, and therefore he sees that all that happens is for his benefit and good.

23.13.3.en: But in spite of this certainty, his human nature, which fears the calamities and pains that come upon him, will not be taken from him. Perhaps this fear or dread is not terror of what will befall him, but the holy fear of the Lord. For he stands in awe before the surpassing majesty and glory of God. He rejoices in the divine presence, but not in negligence or carelessness, rather in reverence and honor toward God.

23.13.4.en: * But you rightly put a question amid these words and say: [O blessed Job, why do you still tremble at sorrows in the midst of such blows? Sorrows have already gazed upon you; you have already been troubled by countless disasters]... But notice how the saint answers our question, adding: "For when He accomplishes His will in me, there are many other things with Him" [14]... With his sight of the incomprehensible power of authority that dwells in Him, the righteous man feels that he is not safe from the blow that comes upon him, and so his fear increases the more.

23.13.6.en: "Therefore am I troubled at his presence:

23.14.0.en: when I consider, I am afraid of him" [15].

23.14.1.en: Job had already declared that he does not tremble before God, because he has boldness toward Him. But here he mentions that he meditates on God's providence and works and fear comes over him, which is the fear of honor and esteem for the Lord, like the fear of a son toward his father.

23.14.2.en: Perhaps what terrifies him is his inner struggle, for in his distress at his friends' accusations against him he finds it good to converse with God and be judged before Him, as though he were saying with David the prophet: "let us fall now into the hand of the LORD; for his mercies are great: and let me not fall into the hand of man" (2 Sam 24:14). And at the same time Job knows that he is not worthy to converse with God and enter into judgment with Him.

23.14.3.en: * "Therefore I am troubled at His presence, when I consider that I am afraid of Him" [15]. He is truly troubled at the presence of the Lord, who sets before his eyes the dread of His majesty and is completely confounded by the awe of His righteousness, seeing that he is not worthy to answer if he is judged strictly...

23.14.4.en: As for blessed Job, we know that he was devoted to offering various sacrifices to God, and gave himself to works of generous giving and to supplying the needs of the poor, and was humble even before those subject to him, gentle with his opponents, and yet such countless disasters befell him... So what shall we say, we wretched creatures? What shall we say, we sinners, if the one who did all this was so afraid?

23.14.6.en: * Nothing is higher than the fear of God, because it rules over everything, and by the fear of God everyone turns away from all evils. Let us acquire this fear for ourselves and turn away from everything that God does not want, and prove all that pleases Him and keep it and do nothing that grieves Him, and know that everything we do He looks at, and nothing is hidden from Him.

23.15.0.en: St. Macarius the Great "For God maketh my heart soft, and the Almighty troubleth me" [16].

23.15.1.en: Although righteous Job had boldness even to enter into judgment with God, he holds to the holy fear, for he perceives the greatness of God and His majesty. Holy love casts out the fear of slaves, but it brings the fear of the Lord, so that the righteous wrap themselves in it before the Holy One. We do not wonder at Job's daring, courage and boldness before God, and at the same time his heart's growing faint and being terrified before the Almighty. This is the way of the children of God: they long with the Apostle Paul to depart and be with Christ and cry out, asking: "Even so, come, Lord Jesus," and at the same time they remember the day of judgment and weep over their sins.

23.15.2.en: * "For God has made my heart faint, and the Almighty has terrified me." It is said that the heart of the righteous man by divine gift becomes faint, as the fear of the coming judgment from the Most High pervades it. What is faint can easily be pierced, and what is hard cannot be pierced. Therefore Solomon says: [Happy is the man that feareth alway: but he that hardeneth his heart shall fall into mischief] (Prov 28:14)...

23.15.3.en: The hearts of the righteous are not secure but troubled, as they think of the great weight of the coming reckoning, and seek to enjoy rest here. They cut off their assurance by thinking of the inner severity. Yet such persons, amid the very chastenings of fear, often remember the gifts, and so they rejoice amid the fears and reconsider the gifts they received to support their hope so that fear subsides.

23.15.5.en: * If you keep in mind the Lord's judgment of the whole earth (Ps 9:7-8), as the Holy Bible says, then every event teaches you the knowledge of God.

23.15.6.en: St. Mark the Ascetic * Remember continually the hour of your departure, and do not forget the eternal judgment, and no sin will be found in your soul.

23.15.7.en: * How do we please God? There are five works that help to bring about God's gift:

23.15.9.en: The second: praise with the Psalms.

23.15.10.en: The third: reading the holy Scriptures.

23.15.11.en: The fourth: man's remembering his sins, death and the fearful judgment.

23.15.12.en: The fifth: work of the hands.

23.16.0.en: St. Mar Evagrius of Pontus "Because I was not cut off before the darkness, neither hath he covered the darkness from my face" [17].

23.16.1.en: Again, although the believer's heart grows faint and is filled with awe, he knows that in the abundance of God's grace he will not perish, and that darkness cannot cover his face as long as he has put his hand in God's hand. By faith the believer sees the gates of heaven open before him, and in watchfulness he fears as he stands, lest he fall, as the Apostle Paul said (1 Cor 10:12).

23.16.2.en: * "But I shall not perish because of the darkness that threatens me, and the darkness will not cover my face"... For the blows that come upon the righteous either remove the evils they practiced, or make them avoid the coming blows that may fall. But blessed Job, when he fell under the rod, was not purified from sins he had committed nor was he fortified against what threatened him. Rather the rod increased his goodness the more while he was under the blow, and so he says with certainty: "For I shall not perish from the darkness that threatens me, and the darkness will not cover my face."

23.16.4.en: Your silence amid my pains is sweeter than the consolations of men!

23.16.5.en: * In the midst of the bitterness of my soul I complained; my pains are heavier than every groan or sigh. He who sees me thinks that I murmur against You.

23.16.6.en: I trust in You, in Your love and Your righteousness.

23.16.7.en: I want to meet You, for You alone search my heart. Why are You silent, O Lover of mankind?

23.16.8.en: Judge me, but according to Your mercy!

23.16.9.en: I want to converse with You, for I know that by Your Cross I am delivered forever.

23.16.10.en: * Why are You silent, O You who are wonderful in Your love?

23.16.11.en: I want to flee from divine justice by taking refuge in Your love.

23.16.12.en: I confess my sins to You, for who has pity on my weakness as You do?

23.16.13.en: * If I look to the east, I see Your greatness.

23.16.14.en: So I fall silent before Your splendor.

23.16.15.en: And if I look to the west, where I draw back before You, my understanding freezes completely!

23.16.16.en: If I walk on the left, where sins are, I cannot comprehend You.

23.16.17.en: And if I walk on the right, where the blows of self-righteousness are, I deprive myself of seeing You.

23.16.18.en: Tell me, how shall I see You and speak with You, for You are my only refuge.

23.16.19.en: * You are in every place, You are in my depths, and in my folly I did not know how to meet You!

23.16.20.en: You see me and search my depths, and because of my blindness I do not see You, nor comprehend Your mysteries!

23.16.21.en: Your plan for me is surpassing.

23.16.22.en: * You want me to be gold refined by fire, without dross; You permit trials for me, and You work in me without ceasing, even if You are silent.

23.16.23.en: Amid my bitter cries, You see my soul being purified as by fire.

23.16.24.en: You see me coming to You in glories that are the work of Your grace in me!

23.16.25.en: In Your silence You seem as one who does not care for my bitter cries, but You, the wise Potter, know when to bring me out of the furnace of trials.

23.16.26.en: You look upon me, the clay, and see me changed into a vessel of honor!

23.16.27.en: You will not leave me in the fire until I am burned, and You will not bring me out before the time lest I be spoiled!

23.16.28.en: * I see You, the heavenly Physician, in Your silence holding the scalpel.

23.16.29.en: Strike my body with it, and remove its sores.

23.16.30.en: I see You as the Father who, though silent, has His eyes upon His beloved son.

23.16.31.en: Now let me walk according to Your incomprehensible purposes.

23.16.32.en: With thanksgiving I receive Your plan for me, however bitter it may seem.

23.16.33.en: Let me keep Your way by Your grace.

23.16.34.en: For You have promised me that I shall be a son of the heavenly Father!

23.16.35.en: * In the midst of the depth of Your love I realize that You alone are the Almighty.

23.16.36.en: Who can understand the depths of Your wisdom?

23.16.37.en: Work in me, even if my soul grows bitter, for all that You do is for my sure edification.

23.16.38.en: I am the weak clay submitting to its mighty Former.

23.16.39.en: Even if I am distressed for a time, Your wonderful majesty captivates my whole being.

23.16.40.en: * You have fixed Your fear within me; it is my fortress and my refuge from the enemy's warfare.

23.16.41.en: In it I take shelter, and by it I walk as is fitting for a son of Yours!
